headline: Franco-Nevada: earnings up a third on $4,250 gold despite 6% fewer ounces; Cobre Panamá talks move a step closer
takeaway: Adjusted EPS rose 33% to $1.89, ahead of the $1.73 consensus, as revenue rose 13% to $549 million on higher gold and oil prices. Gold-equivalent ounces sold fell 6%, below management’s expectations, and the shares slipped 3%. Franco-Nevada has $4.8 billion of available capital and no debt.
results: Franco-Nevada reported revenue of $549.3 million for the third quarter, up 13%, operating cash flow of $429.2 million, up 23%, and adjusted EBITDA of $493.9 million, or $2.56 a share, up 15%. Net income rose 38% to $395.5 million and adjusted net income 33% to $364.5 million, or $1.89 a share.

The royalty company sold 130,435 gold-equivalent ounces (GEOs), down 6%, or 120,857 net GEOs, down 3%. Gold revenue rose to $383.1 million from $351.6 million even though ounces fell to 90,083 from 101,068, implying an average price of about $4,250 an ounce. Oil revenue rose 61% to $48.9 million, while iron ore fell.
For the first nine months revenue rose 45% to a record $1.78 billion and adjusted net income 63% to $6.08 a share. Available capital stood at $4.8 billion with no debt.
mgmt: Chief executive Paul Brink said precious-metal deliveries were slightly below expectations but strong oil prices lifted diversified revenue, and the company is tracking toward the middle of its annual guidance range.

On Cobre Panamá — the Panamanian copper mine shut by government order in late 2023, on which Franco-Nevada holds its largest stream — Brink said First Quantum continued processing stockpiles and that a government commission had recommended formal negotiations with First Quantum on the mine’s future. He also cited progress at Antapaccay, Copper World and Ring of Fire, and a second financing tranche for the Bullabulling gold project in Australia.
view: Franco-Nevada is a different kind of gold investment: it does not mine anything. It pays mining companies upfront in exchange for a share of their future output, which leaves it with revenue that rises with metal prices but costs that do not. That is why net income rose 38% in a quarter when ounces sold fell 6% — almost every dollar of higher gold price falls straight to profit. Miners such as Barrick saw costs per ounce rise more than 20% in the same quarter; Franco-Nevada has no such exposure.

The ounce shortfall is the reason for the share-price dip, but it is a timing issue at specific operations rather than a structural problem, and the company held its guidance. The bigger swing factor remains Cobre Panamá. Before its closure it was Franco-Nevada’s single largest asset, and the recommendation to open formal negotiations is the most concrete progress in three years. A restart would add significant gold-equivalent ounces with no extra investment; continued closure is already reflected in guidance.

The trade-off for this lower-risk model is valuation. Royalty companies trade at a large premium to miners — Franco-Nevada at roughly 27 times trailing earnings — because investors value the cost protection, diversification and balance sheet. With $4.8 billion to deploy and a pipeline it describes as strong, the company’s next growth step will come from deals, and high gold prices make miners more willing to sell streams. For investors who want gold exposure without operating risk, this report confirms the model is doing exactly what it is supposed to.
watch: Watch the formal Cobre Panamá negotiations between Panama and First Quantum, fourth-quarter GEO deliveries against guidance, and how Franco-Nevada deploys its $4.8 billion.
